To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
the Dutch electorate depolarized along with the party system, and that this depolarization extended to the entire electorate, not just to its affluent, educated, engaged segments.
the Dutch public’s policy preferences depolarized between 1986 and 1998, and that this depolarization occurred equally throughout the electorate.

(1) the mass public depoliticized in line with the party elites, (2) this depoliticization was not restricted to the politically engaged and affluent, and (3) the Dutch public's Left–Right policy beliefs and partisan preferences were more polarized than those of the British public, but were less polarized than the publics in the United States and Germany.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the extent to which the public depolarized along with party elites in the Netherlands.
the relationship between the political elites and the public in the Netherlands.
the extent to which citizens’ attitudes towards politics have become more polarized over the course of recent decades.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
there was a general elite depolarization in the 1980–98 period and that the mass electorate depolarized along with the elites.
the Dutch mass public did indeed depolarize along the Left–Right axis during the 1980–1998 period.
the public depolarized, but the parties did not.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the Dutch electorate has become more moderate in its policy beliefs and partisan attachments.
the mass public in the United States and the Netherlands depolarized during the period under study, while the mass public in Britain did not.
the Dutch electorate depolarized along with party elites during the 1980-2002 period.
The main takeaway from our work is that
, when elites polarize in the opposite direction of the public, the latter depolarizes, not because it is more ideologically extreme, but because it is more heterogeneous.
, in the Netherlands, parties’ ideological convergence has not led to a polarization of the Dutch electorate, but has, on the contrary, contributed to a more centrist electorate.
the depolarization of party elites has important consequences for political representation and party strategies.
